script: The Polish army once had a soldier who was six feet tall, covered in fur, and answered to the name Wojtek. In 1942, Polish soldiers moving through Iran met a local boy carrying a tiny brown bear cub. They traded him food for it, and raised the cub in camp. He grew up among them, billeted with the troops and sleeping in their tents, until he stood over six feet tall. Then the unit was ordered to Italy. British rules banned animals aboard the transport ships, so the army found a loophole. Wojtek was given the rank of private, his own serial number, and an army paybook. On paper he was a soldier, not a mascot. At Monte Cassino in 1944 he carried crates of artillery shells to the gun crews. He was promoted to corporal, and his unit put a bear carrying a shell on their badge. After the war he lived at Edinburgh Zoo until 1963. Follow for more true stories that sound completely made up.

metadata.title: Random But True: The Bear Who Was Officially A Soldier
metadata.caption:
In 1942, Polish soldiers moving through Iran traded food to a local boy for a brown bear cub. They named him Wojtek and raised him in camp.

When the unit was ordered to Italy, British transport rules banned animals aboard the ships. So the Polish II Corps found a way around it. They enlisted him. Wojtek was given the rank of private, a serial number and his own army paybook, which made him a documented soldier rather than a mascot.

At the battle of Monte Cassino in 1944 he carried crates of artillery shells to the gun crews. He was promoted to corporal, and his unit adopted an emblem of a bear carrying a shell as their official badge.

After the war he lived at Edinburgh Zoo until his death in 1963, aged 21. Statues of him now stand in Edinburgh and in Krakow.
